lesson.title: Morning to Night Routine
lesson.subtitle: levantarse (me levanto), lavarse, vestirse, acostarse (me acuesto) across a full day

hook.title: From 'Me Levanto' to 'Me Acuesto'
hook.content: Follow the rhythm of a Spanish day: Por la mañana me levanto a las siete ('In the morning I get up at seven'), and por la noche me acuesto a las diez ('at night I go to bed at ten').

pattern.title: Matching the Pronoun on Infinitives: Voy a Levantarme
pattern.content: Watch what happens when you put voy a or quiero in front of levantarse or acostarse: if the subject is 'I' (yo), the -se on the infinitive MUST change to -me! Voy a levantarme temprano ('I am going to get up early') or Me voy a levantar!

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:

matching_pairs.german: a las siete de la mañana

exercises.target_answer: me levanto, te levantas, me acuesto, quiero levantarme, a las siete de la mañana
exercises.meaning: I get up, you get up (tú), I go to bed (o→ue), I want to get up (hooked -me!), at seven in the morning
exercises.explanation: Match the reflexive pronoun to the subject whether it stands before the verb or hooks onto the infinitive!

exercises.prompt: Hook the 1st-person reflexive pronoun ('myself') onto 'levantar' to say 'to get (myself) up':
exercises.explanation: When the subject is 'I', levantarse changes -se to -me: quiero levantarme.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'I want to go to bed now'?
options: Quiero acostarme ahora (or Me quiero acostar ahora)
exercises.target_answer: Quiero acostarme ahora (or Me quiero acostar ahora)
exercises.meaning: I want to go to bed now
exercises.explanation: Because 'I' am the one going to bed, -se becomes -me: Quiero acostarme.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'I get up at seven in the morning'
exercises.target_answer: Me levanto a las siete de la mañana
exercises.meaning: I get up at seven in the morning
exercises.explanation: Me levanto + a las siete + de la mañana (use de la mañana when a specific clock hour is stated!).

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.meaning: I get up at seven o'clock

summary.outcome: Describe morning-to-night routines and adapt reflexive pronouns on infinitives (levantarme, acostarme).

use_example.german: Me levanto a las siete de la mañana y quiero acostarme a las diez.
use_example.english: I get up at seven in the morning and I want to go to bed at ten.

summary.takeaway: With a clock hour, 'in the morning / at night' uses de (a las siete de la mañana); without a clock hour, it uses por (por la mañana)!
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([2402] Non-Literal & Reciprocal Reflexives): see how irse means 'to leave' and nos vemos means 'we see each other'.

twist.prompt: Assemble: 'I am going to get up'
twist.explanation: Voy a levantarme (or Me voy a levantar).

levantarse.english_meaning: to get up (me levanto: I get up)
levantarse.context_translation: I get up at seven o'clock.

acostarse.english_meaning: to go to bed, lie down (me acuesto: I go to bed)
acostarse.etymology_derivation: From costa ('rib/side') = 'to lay oneself on one's side'.

me.etymology_derivation: Walks left of conjugated verbs or hooks onto infinitives.

se.english_meaning: himself, herself, yourself (usted), themselves; to him/her/them (before lo/la)
se.shift_rule: Reflexive AND the 'se lo' replacement for *le lo
se.context_translation: I tell it to him/her today.
se.etymology_derivation: Whenever le or les meets lo/la/los/las, Spanish softens the tongue-twister *le lo into se lo!

nos.english_meaning: us, to us, ourselves, each other

mañana.context_translation: Tomorrow I am going to work.
mañana.etymology_derivation: As an adverb (mañana) it means 'tomorrow'; as a feminine noun (la mañana) it means 'the morning' (mañana por la mañana = 'tomorrow morning')!

noche.etymology_derivation: Latin noctem. The -ct- became Spanish -ch-: octō → ocho, lactem → leche.
